misclassified_entities.original_description: Development teams proposing and coordinating network upgrades
misclassified_entities.reason_for_misclassification: This is a governance/coordination entity that participates in protocol decision-making processes, not an external entity that sends data into the system during runtime. Network upgrade proposals flow through social consensus, not protocol data flows.

misclassified_entities.original_description: Teams implementing the upgrade in Ethereum client software
misclassified_entities.reason_for_misclassification: These are implementation teams that produce client software. They do not send data into the protocol at runtime; rather, they implement the protocol specification. Their influence is through code releases, not data flows.

misclassified_entities.original_description: Operators who must update their nodes before the activation block
misclassified_entities.reason_for_misclassification: Node operators run the infrastructure but do not send data into the protocol as an external entity. They are participants in the network who choose to adopt upgrades, not external data sources.

misclassified_entities.original_description: Entity that deployed the contract bytecode being executed
misclassified_entities.reason_for_misclassification: The deployer's influence ended at deployment time. During contract execution, the deployer is not sending data into the system - the deployed code is already part of state. The actual external entity during execution would be the transaction sender/caller.

trusted_external_entities.entity_description: Transaction that triggers contract execution leading to SELFDESTRUCT
trusted_external_entities.trust_rationale: Transactions can be submitted by any network participant. The transaction sender is not authenticated beyond signature verification, and transactions can contain arbitrary calldata designed to exploit contract vulnerabilities. SELFDESTRUCT-triggering transactions could be crafted maliciously.
trusted_external_entities.authentication_mechanism: ECDSA signature verification only - proves control of private key but not intent or trustworthiness

trusted_external_entities.entity_description: External application requesting transaction submission with ABI metadata
trusted_external_entities.trust_rationale: The specification explicitly acknowledges DApps as 'potentially malicious' and notes that ABI information comes from the DApp, not from verified contract code. DApps could provide misleading ABI to deceive users about transaction intent. The selector validation only ensures consistency between provided ABI and data, not accuracy.
trusted_external_entities.authentication_mechanism: None - DApp is not authenticated, only the transaction signature is verified

trusted_external_entities.entity_description: End user who reviews and approves/rejects the transaction
trusted_external_entities.trust_rationale: User has authenticated to the wallet (typically via password/biometrics) and explicitly makes approval decisions. However, user decisions can be manipulated through misleading UX or ABI spoofing. The user is trusted to make decisions but inputs must still be validated for format/bounds.
trusted_external_entities.authentication_mechanism: Wallet authentication (password, biometrics, hardware key) - authenticates user to wallet but user judgment may be compromised by deceptive UI

trusted_external_entities.entity_description: External entity that provided the call data in the original transaction
trusted_external_entities.trust_rationale: Any network participant can submit transactions with arbitrary calldata. CALLDATALOAD/CALLDATACOPY operate on this untrusted input. The protocol already implements zero-padding for out-of-bounds reads, acknowledging the untrusted nature of this data.
trusted_external_entities.authentication_mechanism: ECDSA signature verification - proves sender identity but calldata content is arbitrary

trusted_external_entities.entity_description: External entity that submitted type-3 transaction with blob versioned hashes
trusted_external_entities.trust_rationale: Blob transactions can be submitted by any participant willing to pay blob gas fees. The blob_versioned_hashes array and blob data are user-provided. The BLOBHASH opcode safely returns zero for invalid indices, demonstrating untrusted input handling.
trusted_external_entities.authentication_mechanism: ECDSA signature - economic commitment via blob gas fees provides some spam resistance but does not establish trust

boundary_edges.data_flow_description: External transaction invokes contract execution, potentially leading to SELFDESTRUCT
DApp supplies ABI metadata that will be used to display transaction details to user
DApp submits RPC request with transaction object and ABI to wallet
User provides approval/rejection decision after reviewing transaction details
Transaction sender provides calldata that becomes available in evm.message.data for CALLDATALOAD/CALLDATACOPY operations
Blob transaction submitter provides versioned hashes accessible via BLOBHASH opcode

coverage_analysis.notes: All valid external entities have identified trust boundary edges. The EIP-1872 governance entities (EXT-CORE-DEVS, EXT-CLIENT-TEAMS, EXT-NETWORK-OPERATORS) and EXT-CONTRACT-DEPLOYER were correctly identified as misclassified since they don't represent runtime data flows.
